title.narrative: NIHR Global Health: Shaping Health Packages And Researching Priorities (SHARP)

description.narrative: Governments' funding decisions for Universal Health Coverage include choosing health services among a wide range of options, varying in costs, health, and societal impacts, within a limited budget envelope. Collating locally relevant evidence on these services and involving key local stakeholders can help governments and national insurers prioritise the health services they fund and provide legitimacy to these choices. One approach to decide which services to fund is to define ‘health benefit packages’ (HBPs). HBPs list the services to be publicly funded and guaranteed to the population. Several countries in Africa and elsewhere have begun adopting processes to assess and review a range of evidence to prioritise their HBPs, considering whether services provide value for money, improve equity, and are feasible to deliver at scale. This priority setting process requires the creation of national structures that organise transparent, expert review of the evidence as well as stakeholder engagement including both public and patient representatives. Informing this process is challenging given the extent of evidence required; the complexity of engaging various stakeholders; and the challenge of ensuring HBPs are adopted by healthcare providers. Our consortium will explore and test approaches to defining HBPs from 2025-2029. Emphasis will be placed on producing evidence under real data, time, and capacity constraints; involving communities and patients; and ensuring linkage between HBPs and service delivery. This research will be embedded in HBP revision processes in Rwanda and Kenya, with the aim of informing the wider African region. Our novel methods will explore the risk of making decisions under weak evidence; acceptability of HBP design; and the implications of HBPs for the health system including challenges to existing interests. Our research will be undertaken by partnership comprising University of Rwanda, University of Nairobi, KEMRI, London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine and Radboud University. The work will strengthen capacity in health systems, economics, and policy analysis, facilitating institutions in Rwanda and Kenya to develop or expand research groups. We will engage communities and support national policy makers to identify technical and policy constraints affecting priority setting and we will work with Africa Center for Disease Control and the World Health Organisation to ensure lessons are shared regionally and globally.

The project has 8 objectives: • To inform and design an approach to selecting the best evidence assessment method for evidence informed priority setting for health benefits packages (HBPs) in Rwanda and Kenya, based on an evaluation of the data, time and resource requirements, the cognitive demands and the risk associated with each method.
• To inform and design strategies for effective patient and community involvement in HBP revision through the identification of the key stakeholders, and determining their interests and preferences.
• To develop an approach to selecting which health systems functions and costs should be considered in HBP design to identify the implications of HBPs for the health system
• To assess whether HBPs achieve the procedural aims of evidence-informed priority setting processes in Rwanda and Kenya.
• To assess the consequentialist outcomes of evidence-informed priority setting processes in HBP design in Rwanda and Kenya.
• To understand how HBPs impact the allocation of resources and power between key actors, including how interests are contested, stated, aligned, and negotiated in Rwanda and Kenya.
• To pilot a self-reflective evaluation for stakeholders involved in evidence-informed priority setting and HBPs to determine 1) how and why priority setting processes succeed or fail; 2) how success or failure relates to underlying interests; and 3) what lessons other countries can learn from Rwanda and Kenya.
• To strengthen training and capacity development and community engagement and involvement for HBP design process in Rwanda and Kenya
